question_text: Bearish Vertical Spread strategy is used to reduce the cost of a long position by selling a lower strike put.

question_text: Basis: The difference between the Spot Price and the Future Price.
explanation: If future price is higher than spot, the basis is positive. [cite: 8]

question_text: Strangle involves buying both a call and a put with different strike prices but the same expiry.

question_text: Straddle involves buying both a call and a put with the same strike price and expiry.

question_text: Time Value: Option Premium - Intrinsic Value

question_text: Periodic investment is only possible if income exceeds Spending (or Liabilities)
hints: Monthly costs, bills, or debt payments.
explanation: Periodic investment is only possible when there is a positive net cash flow. [cite: 3]

question_text: Inflation erodes the purchasing power of money over time.
explanation: Returns must beat inflation to provide real growth. [cite: 7]

question_text: Speculators are market participants who provide liquidity by being open to taking risks.
explanation: Speculators take on risk to provide the liquidity hedgers need to reduce their risk. [cite: 8, 9]

question_text: Mark to Market (MTM): The process of daily margin adjustment based on market prices.
explanation: MTM ensures losses are collected and profits are paid out on a daily basis. [cite: 8, 9]

question_text: Value at Risk (VaR): Margins in the Indian derivative market are based on this methodology at a 99% confidence level.
explanation: As per the Dr. LG. Gupta committee, VaR is used to calculate margin requirements. [cite: 8, 9]

question_text: Impact cost represents the cost incurred during trade execution due to prevailing liquidity conditions
hints: It impacts both buyers and sellers.
explanation: High impact cost increases the buying price and reduces the selling price. [cite: 8, 10]

question_text: SCORES is the SEBI web-based centralized grievance redressal system.
explanation: This system allows investors to track the status of their complaints online. [cite: 8, 9]

question_text: Calendar Spread strategy involves buying an underpriced future and selling an overpriced future of different months.
explanation: This is an arbitrage strategy between contracts with different expirations. [cite: 8]

question_text: Cost of Carry: The relationship between the future price and the spot price.
explanation: For equity, this is interest paid minus any dividends earned. [cite: 8]

question_text: STT (Securities Transaction Tax) is a tax levied on all purchase and sale transactions of listed securities in India
explanation: STT applies to equity, derivatives, and equity-oriented mutual funds. [cite: 8, 11]

question_text: UCC (Unique Client Code) is a unique 10-digit number linked to a client's PAN for identification.
explanation: Brokers must allot a UCC to every client during onboarding. [cite: 8, 10]

question_text: Bid price is the price at which the market is prepared to buy a security.
explanation: The Ask price is where the market is prepared to sell. [cite: 8]

question_text: IDC (Immediate or Cancel) order: any unmatched portion of the order is cancelled immediately.
explanation: This order type does not allow any part of the order to remain in the book. [cite: 8]

question_text: Leverage: Using a small amount of margin to get a large market exposure.
explanation: Leverage allows traders to control large contract values with limited capital. [cite: 8]

question_text: Operational risk includes losses due to internal failures like fraud, strike, or outdated machinery
explanation: This risk arises from an organization's internal activities and processes. [cite: 8]

question_text: Losses on derivative transactions can be carried forward for 8 assessment years.
explanation: This allows traders to set off future gains against past losses. [cite: 8]

question_text: Clearing Corporation acts as a legal counterparty to all trades and guarantees their settlement.
explanation: It steps in as the buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer. [cite: 8]

question_text: Market order is one where the price is not specified at the time of placement
explanation: Market orders execute immediately at the best available prevailing price. [cite: 8]

question_text: Basis risk is the chance that the two future prices will not fluctuate identically during a hedge.
explanation: This risk exists in calendar spreads and other hedging strategies. [cite: 8]

question_text: FIU-IND: Suspicious transactions must be reported here under Anti-Money Laundering regulations.
explanation: The Financial Intelligence Unit-India detects money laundering attempts. [cite: 8]

question_text: Cross Margining allows a trader to use a credit balance in the cash segment to meet margin needs in derivatives.
explanation: This prevents excessive funds from being blocked in different segments. [cite: 8]

question_text: The STT rate for the sale of stock or index futures is 0.0125 percent.
explanation: This rate was revised effective from April. [cite: 8]

question_text: SEBI board members are appointed by the Central Government of India.
explanation: SEBI is the overall regulator for the securities and derivatives market. [cite: 8]

question_text: Settlement means the actual pay-in or pay out to settle the contract.
hints: It is the final stage of the trade cycle.
explanation: Clearing is the calculation of obligations, Settlement is the actual exchange of money/securities. [cite: 9]

question_text: Professional (PCMs) Clearing Members do not execute trades; they only clear and settle trades for other trading members.
hints: Think of a member who acts as a service provider.
explanation: PCMs provide clearing services to Trading Members (TMs) who do not have clearing rights. [cite: 9]

question_text: Speculators provide much-needed liquidity and are open to taking risks.
explanation: Speculators take risks for profit, whereas hedgers enter the market to reduce existing risks. [cite: 9]

question_text: The tick size for USDINR currency futures contracts in India is 0.0025 (or 0.25 paise)
hints: It is a very small decimal value in Rupees
explanation: This is the minimum price movement allowed for USDINR futures on Indian exchanges. [cite: 9]

question_text: For Government Bonds futures, the last trading day is the last Thursday of the contract month.
hints: It's a specific day of the week.
explanation: T-Bill futures expire on the last Wednesday, but Government Bond futures expire on the last Thursday. [cite: 9]

question_text: The minimum net worth required for an authorized exchange of currency futures is Rs 100 crores.
hints: It is a triple-digit round figure.
explanation: Regulatory requirements mandate a high capital base for the exchange itself. [cite: 9]

question_text: VaR (Value at Risk) margins should be based on methodology at a 99% confidence level.
hints: A three-letter acronym starting with V
explanation: VaR is the standard statistical technique used to measure the risk of loss on a portfolio. [cite: 9]

question_text: Systematic risk cannot be controlled or eliminated through diversification.
explanation: Systematic risk (Market risk) is inherent to the entire market. [cite: 9]

question_text: Mark-to-Market (MTM) gains and losses are settled in cash before the start of trading on T+1 day.
explanation: Daily settlement happens the next business day after the trade (T+1). [cite: 9]

question_text: AS 30 is the accounting standard issued by ICAI that defines the accounting for derivatives.
hints: It is a number in the 30s.
explanation: AS 30 specifically deals with the recognition and measurement of financial instruments. [cite: 9]

question_text: Amortized: when a forward contract is used for hedging, the premium or discount should be spread over the life of the contract.
hints: This means spreading the cost/benefit over time
explanation: Per AS-11, the cost or gain is spread across the contract duration. [cite: 9]

question_text: 91-day Treasury Bill: The underlying for the 91-day Treasury Bill futures in India.
hints: The answer is in the name of the contract.
explanation: The 91-day T-Bill serves as the specific benchmark for short-term interest rate futures. [cite: 9]

question_text: FIFO: method used to calculate profit/loss if more than one contract in a series is outstanding at expiry.
explanation: This ensures a standardized chronological approach to squaring off positions. [cite: 9]

question_text: Price-Time: priority followed by exchanges for continuous matching.
hints: The best price gets filled first then the earliest time.
explanation: Orders are matched primarily on the best price available, then time. [cite: 9]

question_text: Passive orders are unmatched buy or sell orders waiting in the order book to be matched.
explanation: Passive orders provide liquidity by sitting in the book. [cite: 9]

question_text: Stop Loss Limit order includes both a Trigger Price and a Limit Price
explanation: Once the trigger price is hit, it becomes a limit order at the specified price. [cite: 9]

question_text: Up (or Rises): When the Indian Rupee (INR) depreciates against the USD, the USDINR pair price goes up.
hints: Think of the exchange rate moving from 80 to 82.
explanation: Depreciation means you need more units of INR to buy one unit of USD. [cite: 9]

question_text: CHF is the symbol for the Swiss Franc in the currency market.
explanation: CHF is the international ISO code for the Swiss Franc. [cite: 9]

question_text: Reserve (or Vehicle) currency: When two currencies are traded against a common third currency.
explanation: Most currency pairs are liquid because they trade against the US Dollar as an intermediary. [cite: 10]

question_text: Buyer: For interest rate derivatives in India, Stamp Duty is levied only on the buyer.
explanation: Unlike the cash market, where it might be shared, in IRDs, the buyer pays the duty. [cite: 10]

question_text: 2 Lakh: Treasury Bill futures in India have a standardized minimum tradable quantity.
explanation: This ensures a minimum contract size for participation. [cite: 10]

question_text: Flattening: When the difference between long-term and short-term interest rates narrows.
explanation: Flattening occurs when short-term rates rise faster than long-term rates or vice versa. [cite: 10]

question_text: PDO (Public Debt Office): The depository for all Government Securities in India.
explanation: The PDO maintains the records of ownership for all government-issued debt. [cite: 10]

question_text: Accrued interest: interest earned by the seller from the last coupon date to the trade settlement date.
hints: It is "earned but not yet paid."
explanation: The buyer compensates the seller for the portion of the interest period the seller held the bond. [cite: 10]

question_text: Modified duration measures how much a bond's price will change for a 1% change in interest rates.
hints: It is "Macaulay duration adjusted for yield.
explanation: Modified Duration is the primary tool for measuring interest rate sensitivity. [cite: 10]

question_text: Initial Margin is the initial deposit required to open a futures position.
explanation: It acts as a safety buffer for the clearing corporation against potential defaults. [cite: 10]

question_text: Impact Cost is the difference between the expected price and the actual execution price due to liquidity.
explanation: High impact cost indicates low liquidity, as large orders move the price against the trader. [cite: 10]

question_text: Naked position means a trader has a directional view without any hedge.
explanation: A naked position carries full market risk, unlike a spread or a hedged position. [cite: 10]

question_text: Segregated (or Separate Client) funds must be kept in a bank account separate from the broker's own money.
explanation: This prevents the broker from using client money for their own trades or losses. [cite: 10]

question_text: Core SGF (Settlement Guarantee Fund) is maintained by Clearing Corporations to guarantee the settlement of trades.
explanation: It acts as a final backstop to ensure trades are paid. [cite: 10]

question_text: Offsetting is the process of ending a futures contract by entering an equal and opposite trade.
hints: Not "Squaring off" but a similar technical term.
explanation: Offsetting cancels out the delivery obligation of the original contract. [cite: 10]
